newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Malaysia poised to buy corn, Thais interested.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia poised to buy corn, Thais interested.

text.p: Malaysia is on the verge of buying one cargo of corn for March/April 1997 delivery and Thailand may also jump in if the price of the staple slips a few more dollars this week or next, traders said on Thursday.
"Malaysia is thinking of at least one Panamax cargo of corn for March/April if the price comes off further," a senior dealer in a European commodity house said.
"If the price comes off by a few more dollars, we're going to see Malaysia and Thailand jump in," a dealer for a U.S. trading house said.

U.S. corn bound for Southeast Asia was quoted by regional traders at around US$146-148 a tonne C&F for February-April delivery on board a Panamax vessel against last week's quote of $145-$150 a tonne C&F for January/February delivery.
Corn was priced at around $170 a tonne C&F in the region between six to eight weeks ago, the traders said.
"The Malaysians are probably going to buy if the corn price dips to $142-$143 a tonne C&F," a dealer for a European trading house said. "The Thais would be close behind them."
Reports of excellent crop prospects in South America may also pressure corn prices lower, prompting buyers here to hang back and wait for further price falls, the traders said.

Corn futures on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) have been dropping steadily over the past few weeks. The December contract fell 1-1-/2 U.S. cents on Tuesday to end at $2.65 a bushel. The contract was above $2.70 a bushel a few weeks ago.
Indonesia is not expected to enter the corn market because it has ample stocks from its own local harvest, traders said.
News that 55,000 tonnes of U.S. heavy grain will be loaded in early December and sail for Malaysia "may be either corn or barley," one trader said.
"It cannot be soybeans or wheat. It's probably a corn shipment," another dealer for a U.S. dealing house said.
On another issue, earlier concerns about moisture in Indian soymeal which held up exports have begun to ease.
"We face the same problem annually although it's a bit more serious this year because of the heavier-than-normal rains in India," one trader said.
Moisture in Indian-origin soymeal reached an average of 10-11 percent when it should be around 7-9 percent or lower, traders said.
"The lower the moisture, the higher the protein content," one dealer said.
"The problem is being solved although it is still an issue in some parts of the country," a U.S. dealer said.
Aside from recent soymeal purchases by Thailand, the rest of the grains and oilseeds market in the region remains quiet, traders said.
Analysts expect regional buyers to field more inquiries from buyers towards the end of the month prior to possibly taking coverage for the March/April period and beyond.
"I think we're going to see a lot more inquiries later in the month," a dealer for a European commodity house said.
"I see the next wave of demand emerging in January or February. I don't expect any demand now. Everything is quiet. It's the right time to go for a holiday," another dealer said.
